78.translation: Therefore, with the intention ‘you should abandon anxiety about kingdom and the rest for your sons,’ he says ‘where.’ On the side of whichever persons—the Pāṇḍavas—the Lord of Yoga, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is present, and where Pārtha, bearer of the Gāṇḍīva bow, is present, there alone is Śrī, royal fortune; there alone is victory; there alone is prosperity, ever-increasing advancement; there alone is policy, right conduct, firm and certain. ‘There’ is to be connected throughout. Thus is my thought, my certainty. Therefore even now, you together with your sons should take refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, propitiate the Pāṇḍavas, offer everything to them, and preserve the lives of your sons. This is the intention. ‘For one endowed with devotion to the Blessed Lord, through knowledge of the Self arising from His grace, release from bondage would easily occur’: this is the summary of the meaning of the Gītā. Indeed, because in passages such as ‘O Pārtha, that Supreme Person is attainable by exclusive devotion’ and ‘by exclusive devotion, O Arjuna, I can be known in this form,’ devotion to the Blessed Lord is heard to be the most effective means toward liberation, it is clearly understood that exclusive devotion to Him alone, furnished merely with the intermediate operation of knowledge arising from His grace, is the cause of liberation. It is proper that knowledge be an intermediate operation of devotion. From statements such as ‘to those who are constantly joined, who worship Me with love, I give that yoga of understanding by which they come to Me’ and ‘My devotee, knowing this, becomes fit for My state,’ it has been said that knowledge of reality itself is devotion. Yet in passages such as ‘equal toward all beings, he obtains supreme devotion to Me; through devotion he knows Me in truth, how great I am and who I am,’ they are designated separately. Nor, if this is so, should contradiction with Śruti passages such as ‘knowing Him alone, one crosses beyond death; there is no other path for going’ be suspected, because knowledge is an intermediate operation of devotion. When it is said ‘he cooks with pieces of wood,’ it is not thereby said that the flames are not a means. And further: ‘For one who has supreme devotion to God, and as to God so to the teacher, to that great soul these meanings that have been taught shine forth’; ‘at the end of the body, the Lord expounds the liberating Supreme Brahman’; ‘He is attained by the one whom He Himself chooses’—Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇa statements such as these become coherent when this is so. Therefore it is established that devotion alone is the cause of liberation. ‘By the understanding given by Him alone this exposition of that Gītā was made. May that very Supreme Bliss, Mādhava, be pleased by it.’ ‘Now, bearing the auspicious dust of the lotus feet of Paramānanda, this Gītā-Subodhinī has been composed by the ascetic Śrīdhara Svāmī.’ ‘Churning the Bhagavad Gītā by the strength of one’s own boldness, can one who seeks the truth contained within it attain it without the nectar-glance of the teacher’s grace? Having cast aside the ocean’s water with one’s own cupped hands, does a person who desires to take its inner jewels not sink in its whirlpools without a good helmsman?’
